This is possible because languages share underlying semantic structure—'water' and 'agua' refer to the same physical concept—so a model trained to align multilingual text can project queries and documents into a shared space where similarity measures work uniformly. This unified space enables the retriever to find relevant documents across language boundaries.
900: The goal is to recommend items to new users whose preference signals have just arrived, while also learning from the accumulating history of how preferences change over time. The foundational principle is that user preferences follow patterns—some stable across all users (like genre preferences), others unique to individuals (like specific movie tastes)—and that separating these shared patterns from person-specific ones lets a model adapt quickly to new arrivals by borrowing the shared knowledge. Separating them works because new user signals cluster around shared preference features even though individual positions along those features vary widely. This separation holds as long as enough new users arrive to reveal the overlap in pattern space. By maintaining this separation and replaying past examples when learning from new users, the model avoids forgetting the shared patterns it learned before, solving the practical problem of giving accurate recommendations on day one for someone who has just signed up.
901: The task is teaching a language model which tool to use for a given user request, starting from imperfect training data where some labeled examples are wrong, some tools are rare, and the tool set itself keeps changing. The underlying principle is curriculum learning: humans learn easier skills before harder ones, and arranging training in that order yields faster mastery than random order. This principle applies here because tool selection has layers of difficulty—basic tool-spotting is easier than disambiguating between similar tools—and a model that masters the easy layer first has a foundation to learn finer distinctions on harder examples. By also screening out genuinely wrong labels and starting with high-quality examples, the model builds correct intuitions that survive introduction of noisier data. This approach avoids the trap of memorizing noise, letting the model generalize to new tools and ambiguous queries it has never seen.
902: Social media events leave traces across images and text that cluster together by theme—a protest leaves a recognizable pattern in both captions and photos—and the goal is to find those clusters without labeled event categories. The core principle is that similarity within a cluster, measured along carefully chosen angles, is stronger than similarity across clusters: if you describe images and text in ways that highlight what makes an event coherent (its theme, its type, what's visually happening), within-cluster pairs will look more alike than random pairs. This principle holds because real events have internal structure—the theme of a protest connects to both its visual markers and how people describe it—and this structure is discoverable without labels by asking a semantic guide (a language model) to describe those features consistently. By forcing the model to make representations that align these descriptions across image and text, the model learns to ignore spurious variation and finds genuine event structure, solving open-world detection without predefined categories.
903: The goal is to predict purchase conversion during promotional events where buyer behavior shifts sharply compared to regular days. The core principle is stable-plus-flexible modeling: some patterns in user behavior (like how engaged they are) persist across both regular and promotional periods, while others (like price sensitivity) shift with the promotion context. If you can identify which patterns are which, you can reuse the stable ones without retraining from scratch and update only the flexible parts. This separation works because the shift from regular to promotional behavior is partial, not a complete reset—user identity and engagement remain, only their decision-making weights shift. By maintaining this split representation and training a fusion mechanism to know when to trust each part in new promotional contexts, the model avoids catastrophic forgetting of regular-day patterns while staying current on promotional shifts, enabling accurate predictions on a day when behavior is genuinely different from yesterday.
904: Large recommender systems use multiple retrieval pathways in parallel to cover different user interests, but these pathways overlap: some items multiple retrievers rank highly, giving little new information. The goal is to identify items only earlier retrievers miss and teach the new retriever to specialize in those, improving total system diversity. The principle is that learning is most efficient when training focuses on gaps rather than already-solved cases: a retriever learning from items everyone ignores learns distinctly from one trained on items everyone retrieves. This principle holds because the training signal in recommendation is sparser than in classification—each user sees few items—so wasting signal on consensus items wastes the precious signal that exists. By identifying truly novel items and teaching the retriever to find them specifically, while encouraging it to avoid stealing items the ensemble already ranks well, the system improves coverage without redundancy, delivering more user interests to the ranker and ultimately lifting user transaction rates.
905: Recommender systems transfer knowledge between product categories (like books and movies) to handle data sparsity, but category-specific words in product descriptions can have different meanings in different categories, breaking knowledge transfer. The goal is to identify which words are truly universal, which are category-specific, and which are category-independent but mean different things across categories. The principle is that meaning depends on context: the word 'action' means 'fast-paced narrative' in movies but 'physical interaction' in video games, and mistaking these for the same concept causes negative transfer. Categorizing words by how concentrated they are within one category versus spread across categories reveals these meanings: concentrated words are category-specific, widespread words are universal, and words somewhere in between may carry hidden domain-specific weight within their category. By respecting these boundaries and connecting only universal knowledge across categories, the model reuses genuine shared patterns while avoiding poisoned transfer from false synonyms, improving recommendations in sparse categories without hurting rich ones.
906: Computing how central each node is in a social network (by the Katz measure) exactly requires tracking influence paths of all lengths, which explodes in cost as networks grow. The goal is to approximate this ranking efficiently on massive graphs. The principle is random walks: if you repeatedly start from a node, take random steps following edges, and count how often you reach other nodes, the hit frequency approximates their true centrality ranking. This approximation works because the random walk process naturally weights paths by their frequency and accessibility—common paths get explored more often—which aligns with how Katz centrality mathematically weights paths, just computed probabilistically rather than algebraically. By running many independent random walks in parallel, computers working on different walks simultaneously, the computation becomes faster by orders of magnitude while maintaining ranking accuracy. This approach trades numerical precision in individual scores for speed and parallelizability, solving the practical problem of identifying influential users in networks too large for exact computation.
907: Search results pages are no longer linear lists but complex layouts where item position, neighbors, and visual design all influence clicks and purchases, yet standard ranking models optimize for position only. The goal is to optimize the entire page experience, including long-term satisfaction like repeat purchases weeks later. The principle is causal effect: measuring what would happen if you placed item A in location 1 versus location 2 requires isolating the effect of placement from all other differences between users who see each position. Quasi-experimental data—users assigned to pages slightly differently—reveals these effects if analyzed carefully. This principle applies because page position affects both immediate click behavior and long-term trust and discovery: a well-placed item may not be clicked today but discover a shopper to a brand they visit later. By using causal reasoning to measure long-term impact and then optimizing page layout for it rather than clicks alone, the model captures the true value of placement and visual emphasis, solving the business problem of sustainable shopper satisfaction rather than optimizing narrow short-term clicks.
908: Generative recommenders that process long user histories produce better recommendations but are slow because they must read and process every past item. The goal is to compress history without losing quality. The principle is that item categories summarize: a user who clicked sports, sports, adventure, adventure has interests in sports and adventure, and those two categories capture their pattern better than six individual item reads. This principle holds because category membership is stable across time while specific items create noise—whether the user clicked 'basketball' or 'soccer' matters less than that they like sports. By grouping items into their category and running the recommender on one instance per category instead of all items, the model reduces computation while preserving the signal about what the user cares about. Experiments show this works as well as much longer histories because the model extracts the true underlying interest without the redundancy of repeated category exposure, solving the deployment problem of making recommendations fast without sacrificing accuracy.
909: Estimating how an individual would respond to an intervention (like a price discount) from network data is hard because people influence each other and confounding factors drive both the decision to intervene and the response. The goal is to disentangle these causes. The principle is that hidden factors divide into roles: some create instruments that justify intervention choices without affecting outcomes (like budget availability), some cause bias by influencing both intervention and outcome (like user wealth), and some affect outcomes only given the intervention. If you can identify these three roles separately, you can measure the intervention effect by adjusting for the confounding factors while preserving the instrumental factors that made the intervention natural. This principle holds because causal structure is identifiable when the roles reflect genuinely different information flows in the data. By learning representations that capture these distinct factors and keeping it simple them to maintain separation, the model recovers the true causal effect sizes even when people influence each other, solving the core inference problem of learning how to optimally target interventions from observational network data.
910: Detecting anomalies in multivariate time series where multiple measurements evolve together is challenging because errors in one measurement compound errors in others if you train the model on all measurements at once. The goal is to improve detection by focusing the model on one target measurement at a time. The principle is concentration: a model trained to minimize error on a single target distributes learning effort entirely on that target, whereas a model trained on many targets dilutes effort across them. This principle applies because each measurement can have anomalies at different times and severities, so a model predicting multiple outputs simultaneously must compromise, fitting some measurements better and others worse. By training separate models for each measurement while only including measurements similar to the target as inputs, the model benefits from related patterns without spreading its error budget. This focused training, combined with access to neighbor patterns that often show anomalies together, gives each model the signal concentration and relevant context it needs to detect subtle anomalies, dramatically improving detection rates on real industrial sensor data.
911: Information extraction from text using AI language systems breaks down when different tasks define entities differently—a 'person' means something different in biography extraction versus clinical notes—and training on multiple definitions causes the model to forget how to handle each one correctly. The goal is to reuse the model's general language understanding while delegating schema-specific mapping to lightweight task-specific models. The principle is separation of concerns: understanding language and identifying named entities is a general skill that applies to all schemas, whereas mapping identified entities to a particular schema's categories is task-specific. These skills are separable because you can identify where 'John Smith' appears in text without knowing whether to call it a 'person', 'subject', or 'entity'; the category assignment is a separate decision. By training the large model only on the general skill (identifying and understanding spans) across all tasks simultaneously, then training lightweight specialists for each schema, the model avoids forgetting one schema when learning another and keeps general ability sharp. This division lets the large model reuse its understanding broadly while allowing each schema to define its own categories, solving the problem of building extraction systems that handle multiple conflicting schemas in production.
912: Self-training for entity recognition amplifies small amounts of labeled data by using a model's own predictions on unlabeled data as new training examples, but the model often predicts wrong and those wrong predictions become training signal, causing errors to compound. The goal is to filter out incorrect predictions before adding them as training data. The principle is that AI language systems have rich knowledge about text and entities that a pure machine learning model lacks, and they can judge whether a predicted entity makes sense given the text's context and actual patterns in the training data. This principle applies because the language model's knowledge comes from diverse text and is orthogonal to the biases the specialized entity recognizer develops. By asking the language model to validate predictions using task rules the language model itself extracted from the labeled data, combined with multiple agreement signals, the model filters pseudo-labels to keep only plausible ones. This careful filtering breaks the error amplification cycle of standard self-training, solving the practical problem of learning entity boundaries accurately from few labeled examples and plentiful unlabeled text.
913: This is a tutorial paper surveying retrieval-augmented generation systems that incorporate structured data like tables, graphs, and hierarchies rather than just flat text. While a tutorial offering structural perspective on RAG design patterns rather than a single method, the underlying principle across all structured RAGs is that structure constrains retrieval: knowing that data lives in a table means you search columns and rows following their edges, knowing it's a graph means you traverse connections, knowing it's a tree means you exploit parent-child relationships. This constraint is sound because external knowledge that is structured does have those boundaries and relationships, and respecting them prevents nonsensical retrieval like matching unrelated tables rows or following broken graph edges. By tailoring retrieval algorithms to the actual structure of each knowledge type rather than treating all knowledge as unstructured text, these systems make fewer spurious retrievals, answer more precisely, and remain more trustworthy in safety-critical scenarios where confidently wrong answers are worse than no answer. The tutorial synthesizes how structure fundamentally improves retrieval quality and safety.
914: Breaking a grid of numbers into its building blocks (rank-1 components) typically uses numerical algorithms with fixed rules for when to stop, but these rules don't adapt to different data characteristics like noise. The goal is to replace those fixed rules with intelligent agents that can decide adaptively when to stop. The principle is hierarchical understanding: when you peel away one rank-1 layer and look at what remains, you can see if it's noise or signal by asking whether its structure is visually coherent—random noise looks like chaos, true signal looks like a pattern. If you can describe what you see in the remaining grid of numbers to an agent and ask it to judge coherence, the agent applies its visual judgment instead of a formula. This principle works because visual coherence is a proxy for presence of real signal that generalizes across different noise levels and grid of numbers types, whereas fixed thresholds are tuned for one noise level and fail on others. By alternating between a language model that proposes the next rank-1 extraction and a vision agent that judges whether the remainder still contains signal worth extracting, the system adapts extraction to the actual structure present, achieving threshold-free deflation that beats fixed-rule algorithms.
915: MerFT grounds meme interpretation by computing how closely a model's answer aligns with oracle evidence while rejecting misleading alternatives. The soundness comes from a matching principle: if you weight answers by how well they connect to real evidence and away from close-but-wrong distractors, the model learns to prefer genuine reasoning over surface patterns. This principle works because memes layer culture, image, and text in ways that superficially similar facts can mislead, so forcing explicit grounding to evidence forces the model to discriminate meaning rather than pattern-match. By thus separating signal from noise in multimodal content, the method solves the real problem of detecting conflict narratives that could spread harmful misunderstandings.
916: The validation protocol measures how energy prediction error from a learned chemical model evolves along real molecular motion trajectories and across composition changes. It works because molecular dynamics explore the actual space of configurations the model must handle, revealing drift or loss of accuracy that static test sets miss. The principle is that a model's true accuracy must be measured in the regime where it will be deployed—here, long-running simulations—not just on isolated snapshot comparisons. When you track error over time and composition without systematic drift, you have evidence the learned model captures real physics, not just memorized benchmarks. This lets chemists and materials scientists trust simulation predictions for digital twins and in-silico design.
917: BidLoop solves multi-hop reasoning by repeatedly asking whether current evidence answers the question, then either retrieving more evidence or stopping. The method works because decomposition and retrieval must cooperate: better subquestions find better passages, which enable better subquestions next. This feedback loop is sound because it breaks a vicious cycle where poor initial evidence leads to weak subquestions, which retrieve irrelevant noise. By making the loop explicit and bidirectional, the framework lets reasoning adapt—if gathered passages are insufficient, the system generates a better subquestion rather than getting stuck. This approach works for complex questions requiring facts spread across multiple documents because it allows the system to learn what evidence it still needs.
918: DyGM preserves knowledge in growing graphs by balancing memory of old facts against learning new ones, weighted by how important each piece is to the graph's structure. The core principle is that not all knowledge decays equally: core structural facts matter more than fringe details, so forgetting should happen selectively. This principle applies because real-world knowledge graphs grow unpredictably in scale and frequency, making uniform treatment fail—if you update identically on rare versus frequent changes, the system drifts. By detecting which facts stabilize the graph's connectivity and explicitly protecting them through replay and reweighting, the method preserves reliability despite chaotic growth. This lets knowledge systems remain useful as they accumulate information over years.
919: ST-KGLP predicts missing links by asking, for each candidate entity, how much it matters in context of the specific query and considering both structural and textual clues. The method is sound because it combines two complementary signals: structure reveals how entities relate within the graph, while text reveals meaning in natural language. Context-aware weighting is the key insight—the same candidate entity deserves different focus depending on what the query emphasizes. This principle works because a query acts as a lens: it highlights relevant aspects of entities and relationships. By computing query-specific focus over candidates, the system avoids treating all evidence uniformly, allowing nuanced reasoning about what link is most plausible given what matters most in context.
920: Building human-aligned AI requires systems that capture what humans express across language, images, and behavior and understand how humans connect within social and semantic networks. The core principle is that human reasoning is multimodal and relational: no single channel—text alone, images alone, or behavior alone—tells the full story. Alignment works because when the system represents the same concepts across modalities and tracks relationships in networks, it can reason consistently across cultural and professional contexts. This principle applies because humans themselves integrate signals across channels and groups; a system that mirrors this structure mirrors how humans actually think. By augmenting and structuring representations this way, the system solves the deeper problem of building trustworthy AI that reasons like humans.
921: ChorusCVR learns conversion likelihood by training on both clicked and unclicked samples, while carefully distinguishing clicked-but-unconverted from truly unclicked users. The method is sound because conversion prediction must face a gap between training and real-world conditions: at training time you only see clicked samples, but at deployment you rank all users. To close this gap without noise, you must split unclicked samples into two kinds—true negatives (the system worked, user just wasn't interested) versus missing labels (no interaction yet). This distinction is the key because it prevents the model from conflating irrelevance with disinterest. By learning robust soft labels that respect this distinction, the method ensures the conversion model generalizes to the full user population at inference time.
922: RURA re-ranks financial recommendations by optimizing for both user adoption and realized returns while respecting user risk tolerance. The core principle is that a good recommendation must survive contact with reality: a user must adopt it and the asset must perform. This two-objective approach is sound because maximizing relevance alone ignores outcomes, while maximizing returns alone ignores user tastes and limits diversification. By computing expected utility for each user (factoring their risk tolerance and likelihood of adoption), RURA balances these competing goals. The method works because it keeps diversity intact while trading minimal ranking loss for real gains in return, solving the practical problem of building recommenders that users trust because recommendations actually pay off.
923: GNN Explainers 2.0 shifts from one-time final explanations to layer-wise tracing and multi-faceted insights that let users query how decisions formed. The core principle is that black-box explanation must mirror how practitioners actually debug: layer by layer, asking not just what the output was but how intermediate steps led there. This principle is sound because understanding a single output mask tells you little; understanding the flow of information through layers tells you where errors enter. A user-centric approach works because different stakeholders need different views—data scientists need technical layer-wise traces, while non-technical users need accessible counterfactual reasoning. By providing configurable, queryable explanations that trace propagation through the model, the method solves the accountability problem.
924: SimTranGCN transfers user preferences across domains by building a similarity grid of numbers that infers target-domain preferences from source-domain history. The core principle is that if you can measure which items in one domain are similar to items in another, users' tastes for source items predict tastes for analogous target items. This transfer is sound because similarity is transitive: if user liked item A in domain one, and item B in domain two is similar to A, then the user likely values item B. This principle applies to cold-start scenarios because new users in the target domain haven't generated data yet, but their source domain history is a signal. By using item similarity as a bridge, the method avoids expensive computation while solving the cold-start problem.
925: Sequential recommendation improves by predicting user intent from search queries, which reveal what the user is actually seeking beyond what browsing history shows. The core principle is that intent is the ground truth that drives both search and shopping behavior; search queries are explicit signals of what matters now. This principle is sound because a user's search history reveals decision-making intent that browsing alone does not—you search for what you want to find. By incorporating query predictions and actual search results into sequential recommendation, the model learns to anticipate the user's next need rather than extrapolating browsing patterns. This approach works because it captures the forward-looking intent driving behavior, not just backward-looking correlations.
926: RPE4Rec retrieves items efficiently by encoding short-term co-occurrence patterns—which items users interact with in close succession—using lightweight relative position information. The method is sound because recent interactions reveal dynamic preference shifts more than overall history; short-term co-occurrence patterns capture the current shopping moment. Relative position encoding captures this efficiently because it measures distance between interactions without storing full historical sequences, reducing computational cost. This principle works because user preferences drift over time—what mattered yesterday may not matter today—so systems must weight recent signals more heavily. By encoding position efficiently in a low-cost module, the method solves the scalability problem while improving relevance for dynamic recommendations.
927: ARCHER distills a large hypergraph model into a lightweight student by using confidence-weighted error guidance and learning from both the teacher and the student's own internal features. The core principle is that a student learns best by combining external feedback (the teacher's outputs) and internal discovery (patterns the student finds itself). This principle is sound because over-relying on teacher feedback can suppress the student's independent learning capacity; balancing both forces the student to extract useful patterns. Confidence weighting applies because not all teacher signals are equally reliable—high-confidence predictions deserve more weight than uncertain ones. By adding a reinforcement learning module to dynamically balance multiple objectives, the method prevents any single signal from dominating training, allowing the lightweight student to develop richer internal representations than static distillation produces.
928: FairData synthesizes a training dataset that promotes fair model outcomes by matching how well a randomly initialized model learns on synthetic data to how it learns on original data, while explicitly encouraging group fairness. The method is sound because dataset construction happens before model training, so biases baked into data propagate through any downstream model. By optimizing synthetic data to match original learning dynamics while keeping it simple for equitable outcomes across groups, the approach ensures the model has fair training material. This principle applies because historical data encodes societal biases that no amount of model tuning can fully correct; the fairness must begin at the data stage. This data-centric strategy solves the fairness problem by making it model-agnostic—any downstream model trained on fair data inherits fairness automatically.
929: ZPT classifies nodes in text-attributed graphs with no labeled examples by training a joint model of graph and text, then generating synthetic training examples for each class from the class name alone. The core principle is that if a model can learn the joint distribution of nodes and their text descriptions together, it can generate plausible examples of any class based purely on semantic meaning. This principle works because the graph and text encode complementary structure: graph topology reveals relationships, while text reveals meaning. By learning to generate both graph and text numeric fingerprints jointly conditioned on class semantics, the model synthesizes useful training examples without real labeled data. This approach solves zero-shot classification by letting the model reason from semantics and structure rather than relying on examples.
930: The core challenge is predicting purchase behavior when different customer groups have fundamentally different buying patterns. The method automatically divides features into two groups: some guide the main prediction model, while others steer how that model adapts itself for each group. The soundness comes from a simple principle: if you let different features drive prediction separately from driving adaptation, you avoid forcing the model to optimize conflicting goals at once. When a feature tries to both predict directly and adjust model weights, the system sends mixed signals during learning. By partitioning the work, each feature set focuses on what it does best, letting the adaptation mechanism discover which groups truly exist in the data rather than guessing from starting guess assumptions about customer segmentation.
931: Synthetic data quality depends on how the data generation mirrors real-world patterns. This work compares two directions: generating diverse raw data first then labeling it (causal), versus numeric fingerprints the target label in the prompt and generating specifically to match that label (anticausal). The principle underlying causal ordering is that forcing a language model to generate data backward from labels creates an artificial shortcut—the model learns to describe the label directly rather than the underlying features that caused it. Real data contains messy correlations and variations beyond what the label captures; anticausal synthesis skips that diversity. Models trained on causal synthetic data see richer patterns because the generation process matches how real data forms, making the trained models generalize better to unseen examples that contain the natural complexity that labels alone cannot capture.
932: The core issue is that AI language systems carry internal beliefs that can contradict external evidence when fact-checking. The method estimates what the model knows versus doesn't know through confidence signals, then adapts evidence retrieval based on those boundaries. The principle is that a model performs most reliably when it stays in its zone of actual knowledge; if it claims high confidence incorrectly (a known human bias), gathering evidence cannot override a false internal certainty. By treating the model's confidence as a signal for what evidence to fetch, and then using causal methods to isolate how internal knowledge influences reasoning, the system avoids cases where the model overrides correct evidence with wrong internal knowledge. This works because it separates the model's knowledge boundaries from its reasoning process, preventing false confidence from contaminating the fact-check result.
933: The problem is estimating causal effects in knowledge graphs where data is incomplete and entities influence each other. The approach reformulates this as two linked prediction tasks: filling missing attributes and estimating treatment effects while accounting for interference between connected entities. The principle is that if you handle missing data and interference together through a unified learned representation, you can estimate effects that remain valid even when the data is sparse. Graph methods work here because they explicitly model which entities affect which others; by letting information flow through the graph structure during learning, the system discovers interference patterns that affect causality estimates. Missing attributes get filled consistently with these relational patterns, so the final causal estimates account for the true dependencies rather than treating each entity in isolation or naively ignoring missing information.
934: Phishing websites try to mimic legitimate sites, so detection must recognize subtle differences in domain structure and content. The method combines AI language systems and traditional machine learning tools to classify domains as phishing or safe. The principle is that different model families capture different signals: traditional models learn from explicit structural features like domain age and certificate properties, while language models understand deceptive writing patterns and social engineering tactics embedded in site content. By comparing what each model type sees, the system builds robustness—if one model is fooled by a particular deception, another model trained on a different type of signal can catch it. This works because phishing involves multiple types of deception (technical spoofing plus human manipulation), and no single approach detects all variants equally well.
935: Sequential recommendation needs to guess what users will click next given their history. The method uses diffusion models (a generative approach that builds structure by gradually removing noise) while numeric fingerprints both implicit information (learned user behavior patterns) and explicit information (known user-item interactions). The principle is that diffusion gradually reveals structure, so you can steer that unfolding process using explicit knowledge to avoid learning spurious patterns. Implicit signals capture what behaviors actually correlate with interest; explicit signals constrain the generation to only plausible user-item pairs. By conditioning the diffusion on both simultaneously, the model learns to extend sequences in ways that honor what it knows about real interactions while remaining open to novel discoveries. This avoids oversimplifying behavior into a single summary, preserving the temporal structure that makes sequential prediction work.
936: Causal learning is rapidly expanding with many algorithms but no consistent benchmarking standards, making it impossible to know which methods work best for which problems. The workshop aims to systematize benchmarks for causal methods, establishing agreed-upon datasets, evaluation metrics, and test scenarios. The principle is that scientific progress depends on reproducible, shared comparisons; without standardized benchmarks, each paper optimizes against different criteria, creating illusions of superiority rather than genuine advances. By defining benchmark tasks in causal discovery and causal inference consistently, the community can measure what each algorithm actually excels at and identify which problems remain unsolved. This works because it aligns incentives toward real algorithmic improvements rather than gaming evaluation metrics, enabling fair algorithm selection and guiding where future research should focus.
937: Academic search (finding papers to read, cite, or review) requires combining diverse signals: citation links, abstract content, and semantic similarity. The Scholar API provides a unified interface to multiple numeric fingerprints—some learned from deep models adjust on citations, others computed via spectral methods on the citation graph structure. The principle is that different numeric fingerprints capture different notions of relatedness: citation-aware numeric fingerprints reflect what researchers actually build on, while spectral methods reveal hidden groups in the research landscape. By letting users combine numeric fingerprints flexibly, the system lets them optimize for their specific task: reviewers benefit from citation structure, authors seeking related work benefit from semantic similarity, funding agencies benefit from identifying emerging research clusters. This works because no single numeric fingerprints captures all aspects of scholarly relevance simultaneously.
938: Machine unlearning tries to remove a person's data from a trained model without retraining from scratch, which is important for privacy. The fundamental challenge is measuring whether the influence truly disappeared—most datasets designed for this lack enough identity-specific variations to catch when a model generates false information instead of actually forgetting. The method establishes three measurable criteria: reducing how often the model mentions a specific person, removing their identity from generated captions, and maintaining overall caption quality. By creating a large dataset with multiple captions per person (some naming them, some not, some detailed versus summary), the evaluation can quantitatively check each criterion. This works because it forces unlearning methods to prove they actually erased identity information rather than just pausing brief outputs; the varied captions reveal whether models truly forgot or merely suppressed certain patterns.
939: The workshop focuses on graphs as a model for web-scale data (links, social networks, knowledge bases) and how to reason over them reliably. Modern graph methods combine structured graph reasoning with language understanding, but ensuring such systems remain interpretable and trustworthy at scale is difficult. The principle underlying reliable graph analytics is that transparent reasoning paths matter: users need to understand why the system recommended a person as reviewer, flagged content as misinformation, or identified a research trend. This works because graphs at web scale serve human ends—editorial decisions, policy recommendations, research guidance—where blind accuracy without interpretability creates risk. By grounding graph analysis in explainability and addressing social goals explicitly (misinformation detection, human-AI collaboration), systems can be both effective and aligned with real needs rather than optimizing only for numerical performance.
940: Bundle recommendation (suggesting sets of items together) is hard when bundles are new because models have no direct examples to learn from. The method mines user-item and bundle-item relationships to infer which users are likely interested in which new bundles, then uses contrastive learning to build robust representations that work in both cold-start and warm-start scenarios. The principle is that new bundles share items with popular ones; if you understand how users relate to individual items and how items compose bundles, you can predict interest in new combinations without direct training data. By comparing positive bundles (ones users actually want) against negative ones (similar but not chosen), the model learns what makes a bundle appealing relative to alternatives. This works because bundle preference is determined by item composition and user taste, both of which exist in the historical data even if specific bundles don't.
941: Taxonomy completion automatically places new concepts into a hierarchy by predicting which existing parent-child relationship they fit into best. The method improves this by generating harder negative examples during learning—instead of using random incorrect positions as negatives, it uses a diffusion model to synthesize increasingly difficult false placements. The principle is that learning improves when contrasts are meaningful; if the model only learns to distinguish true positions from obviously wrong ones, it remains brittle against ambiguous cases. By generating negatives that are semantically close to correct answers but still wrong, the model learns finer distinctions necessary for accurate placement. This works because the hardness of negative examples directly determines what boundaries the model learns; mixing easy and hard negatives teaches the model to discriminate subtle semantic differences between related concepts, making it robust to genuinely difficult classification decisions.
942: Sequential recommendation via diffusion models faces two problems: the generation process can drift (producing recommendations that stray from the user's actual preferences), and real data contains noise that corrupts the learning process. The method adds two fixes: using a learned language systems designed to extract user preference signals cleanly, and constraining the diffusion process to stay on a geometric surface that represents valid user-item relationships. The principle is that diffusion generates by gradually denoising, but without guidance this denoising can follow false patterns created by sparse data. By respecting the geometric structure of user-item space (where valid preferences form a low-dimensional surface), the diffusion stays anchored to realistic sequences even in high-dimensional settings. This works because user preferences follow natural clustering patterns; forcing the diffusion to move along these natural clusters rather than through empty space prevents drift and improves stability.
943: Social media shapes behavior through emotional contagion—when people see others' emotions, those emotions spread and influence their own responses. The talk analyzes this by detecting emotions in online text and tracing how they correlate with behaviors like polarization, engagement, and identity formation. The principle is that emotions act as carriers of social influence; when you measure the emotional tone of interactions, you can see how affect flows between people and populations. Different groups show different emotional signatures: in-group communication emphasizes shared joy and loyalty, while out-group interactions contain anger and dismissal, creating emotional barriers that drive polarization. This works because emotions are drivers of human focus and decision-making; by quantifying emotional dynamics, researchers can explain observed social phenomena (polarization, misinformation spread, group formation) as emerging from emotional processes rather than treating them as separate from how people actually think and decide.
944: Electronic health records contain vast information but it's scattered, redundant, and often irrelevant to specific medical predictions. The method rewrites raw records into summaries optimized for a particular clinical task (like predicting hospital readmission), then trains both the rewriter and the predictor end-to-end using synthetic guidance based on what features clinicians know matter. The principle is that not all health information equally informs every decision; a summary effective for predicting readmission differs from one useful for infection risk. By training the rewriter specifically to highlight features that improve prediction, the model learns what information to compress and what to preserve. This works because clinical knowledge about which factors drive specific outcomes can guide the learning process; synthetic labels built from domain expertise act as a compass, telling the model which records are well-rewritten, so it learns to extract signal rather than noise from the sparse, high-dimensional raw data.
945: The core task is capturing and explaining diverging opinions in a document collection. The soundness rests on a simple principle: partition documents by relevance first, then select evidence from each partition. This works because opinions cluster — documents backing the same position tend to cite similar reasons, so grouping by relevance to the majority view naturally isolates dissenters. By anchoring to the majority, the system creates a stable reference point that makes minority views comparatively easy to find and explain. This let them produce summaries where each claim has concrete evidence attached, solving the real problem that generic summaries hide where disagreement actually lives.
946: The task is detecting when time series behave strangely—spikes, drops, or shifts that signal problems. The approach covers detection algorithms ranging from 1980s methods to modern approaches, plus a hard insight: most automated model selection fails to beat random guessing, which means the field lacks a principled way to choose the right detector for each dataset. This matters because time series anomalies have many sources—sensor faults, supply shocks, fraud—and no single algorithm suits all. By reviewing both classic and modern methods alongside this sobering lesson about selection, they provide a foundation for future work to build detectors that actually know which tool fits which problem.
947: The core problem is retrieving facts from a knowledge graph reliably to answer questions. The soundness lies in treating retrieval as planned search, not heuristic guessing. By analyzing the question first to infer what paths through the graph matter, the system constrains exploration—it asks only the questions that matter and stops when constraints are satisfied. This works because knowledge graphs are structured: facts link in predictable ways, and knowing what to look for lets you avoid exploring dead ends. This transforms RAG from a fuzzy matching game into auditable reasoning, solving the real problem that current systems generate answers that look plausible but can't explain how they arrived there.
948: Graph systems that learn from examples combine a node's features with its neighbors' features by averaging them together—aggregation. The problem is that averaging erases detail: if features start diverse, averaging makes them similar, and if neighbors have different importance, averaging treats them the same. The fix has two parts: before averaging, reshape the features to stay diverse; after averaging, add back information about neighbors' importance. This works because the loss comes from the averaging step itself, and both fixes directly counteract that. By solving information loss, they preserve the detailed structure of the graph, solving the real problem that networks were losing track of important differences in how connected each node truly is.
949: The task is recommending items and explaining why. When a language model retrieves passages about an item, many are irrelevant noise. The solution uses chain-of-thought reasoning to filter: first identify the item that fits the user's needs, then identify which features of that item justify the recommendation. This works because breaking the selection into steps lets the model focus at each stage—first deciding what to recommend, then justifying it—rather than guessing which retrieved facts matter all at once. By staging the selection, they reduce the noise each step must handle, solving the real problem that retrieved knowledge helps only if the model knows which pieces actually support the recommendation.
950: Label propagation spreads labels through a graph by diffusing them along edges until they stop changing. When the graph is dense but compact—meaning its structure arises from a small set of hidden coordinates—storing all edges wastes memory. The insight is that diffusion in this numeric fingerprints space is mathematically identical to diffusion in the full graph, but computing in the numeric fingerprints space avoids ever building the edge list. This works because grid of numbers algebra guarantees that the diffusion process depends only on the eigenvectors of the adjacency, which the numeric fingerprints captures exactly. By computing in the numeric fingerprints space, they make label propagation tractable for graphs with millions of nodes, solving the real problem that dense graphs are too large to fit in memory.
951: This is a position paper on how personalization is evolving from predicting what users want to reasoning about what users should discover. The soundness rests on an observation: prediction-based systems reinforce existing habits, but reasoning-based systems can surface insights users miss. This shift matters because prediction works well when behavior is stable, but it fails when the goal is growth or surprise. By combining reasoning with multi-modal and speech understanding, systems can infer not just what users like, but what they might value learning. This opens a path toward personalization that doesn't trap users in filter bubbles, solving the real problem that recommendation has historically made the world narrower, not wider.
952: Multimodal recommendation systems usually process images, text, and audio separately, then blend their signals. When modalities go missing, this design breaks—alignment fails and imputation adds noise. The solution projects all available modalities into a shared semantic space early, then aggregates only what's present. This works because pretrained models already understand cross-modal meaning, so two modalities can align without a third, and a single modality alone provides useful signal. By fusing early and ignoring what's missing, the system remains robust to incomplete data, solving the real problem that real-world content is messy and recommenders built for perfect data fail in deployment.
953: Code vulnerability detection aims to find bugs that attackers can exploit. Sequence-based models miss the deep structure of code; graph methods capture syntax trees but miss semantic meaning. The solution combines three ideas: represent code as a graph to preserve control flow, use unsupervised learning to find hidden patterns in that graph structure, and enrich nodes with semantic numeric fingerprints from a language model. This works because vulnerabilities depend on both structure (where execution can go wrong) and semantics (what the code intends). By layering all three, the model learns both the dangerous patterns and their meanings. This lets them trace vulnerabilities precisely, solving the real problem that shallow features miss the intricate ways real exploits work.
954: Recommender systems work well for returning users but fail for newcomers—cold-start problem. The solution uses a manager agent that routes new users to semantic search and returning users to personalized ranking. This works because the two populations have opposite needs: returning users have history and benefit from personalization, while newcomers need diverse, discoverable recommendations where collaborative history doesn't exist. By routing to the right method for each user state, the system avoids forcing one approach to solve two different problems. This trades some accuracy for discovery on cold-start, solving the real problem that monolithic recommenders can't serve both groups well simultaneously.
955: Detecting false information is harder when AI language systems generate it fluently and persuasively. Different sources—humans versus AI language systems—need different retrieval strategies to find contradicting evidence. The solution trains a mixture-of-experts network via reinforcement learning to decide when and how much to retrieve for each input, without knowing its source. This works because the network learns to recognize semantic patterns that signal when retrieval helps: uncertain human claims need different evidence than confident AI language systems hallucinations. By adapting dynamically to each input, the system avoids a fixed strategy that works poorly for some sources. This improves accuracy while keeping search cost low, solving the real problem that veracity assessment must handle both human and synthetic falsehoods.
956: A trained hyperdimensional computing model is intellectual property worth protecting, yet attackers can steal it by querying it and observing outputs. The approach generates synthetic data matching HDC's natural biases, queries the target model on that data to get output labels, then trains a copy that mimics those labels. This works because the synthetic data ensures the stolen model learns the same decision boundaries as the original—if the copy agrees with the target on the generated data, it will generalize the same way. This transforms a black-box stealing problem into supervised learning on synthetic examples. This demonstrates a real security risk: even data-free attacks can replicate proprietary models, solving the problem that model theft was thought to need training data.
957: Search engines show different results to different locations, creating filter bubbles where users see only local viewpoints. The analysis uses language models to annotate search results from multiple geographic perspectives, then compares what results users in different regions see. This works because language models can represent diverse interpretations of a topic—right-wing, left-wing, neutral—and label results accordingly. By applying multiple perspectives consistently, the analysis reveals whether personalization algorithms hide disagreement or surface it. This systematic comparison, repeated across locations and topics, builds evidence of where filter bubbles form. This exposes how search engines shape what people discover, solving the real problem that algorithmic curation is usually invisible.
958: Financial markets are driven by unstructured web data—news, regulatory filings, social media—but extracting actionable hypotheses is slow and subjective. The framework combines information extraction and knowledge graphs to identify factual claims, retrieves relevant claims for a user's question, and tests trading rules against historical data. This works because each stage removes noise: extraction finds claims, retrieval filters to relevant ones, and backtesting validates that the claim predicts price moves. By chaining these stages, the system turns messy text into quantifiable hypotheses. This automation lets humans test thousands of ideas instead of dozens, solving the real problem that financial insight is locked in text that markets move too fast to read.
959: Different AI models have different strengths and blind spots—one excels at reasoning, another at factual recall, another at creativity. Showing multiple models side-by-side lets users choose perspectives that fit their needs and vote on which they prefer. This works because diverse models collectively see more than any single one, and aggregating user votes reveals which models actually help people make better decisions. By structuring the choice explicitly, the system shifts from comparing models on benchmarks to comparing them on real-world value. This crowdsourced ranking exposes model trade-offs, solving the real problem that leaderboards based on fixed datasets miss how models perform on the questions people actually care about.
960: The method decomposes time series into trend and periodic oscillations using sums of sines and cosines. This works because these trigonometric functions form a complete mathematical basis—meaning any smooth periodic signal can be expressed as a weighted combination of them, a principle from harmonic analysis. The key insight is that real physical phenomena like climate cycles genuinely ARE built from underlying oscillations at different frequencies that repeat predictably. By learning which frequencies are present and how strong each one is, plus accounting for time shifts unique to each frequency, the model directly captures the repeating pattern structure that explains the data. This lets the system make accurate forecasts for new time periods without needing complex learned rules.
961: Advertising platforms face a timing mismatch: they decide bids immediately after clicks but only observe true purchase outcomes hours or days later, forcing them to guess about delayed conversions. Survival analysis models the probability that a purchase will eventually occur, given how much time has passed since the click—it naturally handles incomplete information about future events. The mathematical guarantee is that survival curves respect monotonicity and properly account for the passage of time as information arrives. By accurately predicting which delayed clicks will convert before they actually do, the platform can set bid prices correctly upfront instead of learning through costly mistakes. This transforms guesswork into principled forecasting.
962: Real recommendation systems operate in stages that influence each other: how items are collected as candidates affects what models learn, and what the model learns changes what gets ranked and shown. The method treats all three stages as a connected whole instead of independently optimized pieces. The soundness principle is that implicit relationships between users, products, and actions carry predictive signal—if you capture these structured relationships once during preparation, condition training on them consistently, and adapt them at serving time, the system converges toward choices that cohere across the full pipeline. This avoids the costly situation where each stage second-guesses the previous one, instead building mutual reinforcement.
963: Friend recommendation in massive social graphs requires handling millions of users and connections, which traditional graph algorithms cannot scale through. The approach borrows a proven technique from language understanding: treating local subgraphs (friends' friends) as sequences to process through specialized text-understanding models. This works because both domains have the same structure—entities in context, relationships between nearby elements—and pre-trained models learn transferable reasoning about "who connects to whom" from scale. The guarantee is that learned language systems models excel at capturing contextual relationships in sequences, and a social network is exactly that: a sequence of local connections. Efficiency follows because these models are built for handling large-scale sequential patterns.
964: Recommendation systems naturally narrow recommendations to a user's primary interests because optimizing only for accuracy rewards showing more of what users definitely like. Calibration enforces a constraint: recommendations should match the actual proportion of user interests across categories, preventing over-concentration. The mathematical foundation is that user preferences are genuinely multi-faceted—users care about multiple topics in different amounts—and ignoring the lesser interests is missing real intent even if it temporarily boosts engagement metrics. By requiring output proportions to match input proportions, the system respects the user's actual interest distribution. Over time, this honest representation prevents filter bubbles and captures the full range of what users actually want to discover.
965: Graphs change over time as new users join and relationships form, yet models trained once forget old patterns when learning from new data—a catastrophic erosion called catastrophic forgetting. The method maximizes mutual information between representations learned in consecutive time periods, ensuring they stay aligned. The principle is that representations capturing overlapping information preserve understanding of stable structures in the graph. By keeping numeric fingerprints from different time periods mutually informative, the model maintains continuity: new information refines old insights rather than erasing them. This built-in continuity constraint prevents the collapse that occurs when learning ignores what came before.
966: Users bundle items for strategic reasons—adding filler to meet shipping thresholds—creating patterns that existing methods confuse with genuine preferences. The framework uses diffusion models, which build up complex patterns by starting with noise and gradually adding structure, to learn purchasing behavior across space and time. Information bottleneck theory then acts as a mathematical sieve: it enforces which signals flow through and which get filtered out, letting the system learn exploratory versus repetitive patterns separately. The guarantee is that information theory quantifies information flow precisely, so constraining flows forces specific decomposition. By explicitly separating these two behavior types mathematically, the model understands the actual drivers behind purchases rather than treating all items as equally intentional.
967: Conversational AI systems often contradict themselves implicitly—saying something now that conflicts with earlier statements or commonsense rules about a stated persona—but catching these requires understanding what should be true about a consistent character. Building a commonsense knowledge graph about personas creates an explicit map of which statements align with which personas. The method then recognizes responses that violate this map and rewrites them into consistency. The soundness principle is logical coherence: if a system's outputs all respect the same implicit rules, they will appear consistent. By making rules explicit and measurable, the system can detect and fix violations before they confuse users. This transforms persona consistency from an implicit hope into an explicit, verifiable property.
968: Inverse propensity scoring reweights training data to correct for selection bias—situations where certain items are shown more often to certain users than the true data distribution warrants. However, reweighting can harm performance if some items become overweighted, and the real benefit often comes from the learning richer representations across multiple tasks simultaneously. The analysis reveals that the actual mechanism isn't just unbiased risk reduction but rather the diversity of learning signals created by trying to predict multiple things at once. This multi-task diversity organically improves how well the model generalizes. Understanding the true mechanism matters because it suggests focusing directly on learning diverse representations rather than chasing the promise of unbiasedness alone, avoiding reweighting pitfalls.
969: E-commerce queries are ambiguous and product catalogs constantly change, making static expansion rules fail. The system trains a language model through a loop: propose query expansions, watch which results users click on from the expanded search, and adjust predictions based on real system feedback. The mathematical principle is reinforcement learning: if a choice produces a reward, increase the probability of making that choice again. The guarantee holds because the search engine provides unambiguous feedback—users interact with retrieved results, showing which expansions actually worked. By iteratively improving choices based on real-world outcomes rather than guessing from training data alone, the system converges toward expansions that match current products and user behavior. This eliminates the gap between offline training and production reality.
970: Language models work well for sequential recommendation but are too large and slow for devices with limited memory and computational power. Singular value decomposition breaks down model parameters into a small set of core components that capture most of the original information while discarding redundancy—achieving compression mathematically proven to retain essential structure. Combined with tokenization normalization that prepares the remaining parameters to work smoothly together, this significantly shrinks the model. Progressive alignment then refines compressed layers one by one, maintaining accuracy as compression increases. The guarantee is that most redundancy in large models is noise; removing it carefully preserves the core functionality. This lets powerful sequential reasoning run on phones without rebuilding from scratch.
971: Graph systems that learn from examples assume connected nodes share similar properties (homophily), but real networks have bridge nodes—connectors between different groups—where neighbors have opposing properties, violating this assumption and breaking the model. The approach identifies these critical nodes and applies a different aggregation rule that prevents smoothing away important differences. The principle is that information smoothing, which works well among similar nodes, becomes harmful when neighbors actually disagree. By measuring which nodes are bridges using graph structure alone and treating them specially, the system avoids the mathematical pathology that sinks standard models. Preserving differences where they matter prevents the false consensus that kills performance on heterogeneous networks.
972: New users with no history pose a cold-start problem: traditional graph and sequence methods have nothing to learn from. The approach combines text descriptions with graph structure—both describe the same entities from different angles. learned language systems models excel at extracting meaning from language, so treating product descriptions as sequences to understand alongside their graph positions creates multiple views of each entity. The principle is that the same entity looks similar in both text space and structure space if you've learned good representations, and forcing alignment between views amplifies the shared signal. This redundancy provides signal even when interaction history is absent, grounding the system in inherent properties rather than behavioral history.
973: Cold-start sequential recommendation breaks when users lack history because models have no behavioral patterns to learn. The system first isolates the user's interactions most likely to reveal true preferences, filtering noise from accidental clicks. Then it uses causal inference to identify which factors actually drive purchasing behavior versus which just correlate, and conditions a diffusion model on these true drivers to generate realistic synthetic behavior. The guarantee from causal logic is that conditioning on causes, not mere correlations, produces realistic predictions because causes are the generative mechanism. By identifying true preference drivers and using them to seed behavior generation, the model creates believable cold-start user profiles. This transforms missing history into generated-but-grounded alternatives.
974: This is a workshop, not a research paper with a technical contribution, so no deep mathematical "why" applies—it's a venue announcement. The workshop aims to connect researchers and industry practitioners working on generative AI applications in streaming media services, facilitating knowledge exchange rather than proposing a novel method with mathematical guarantees.
975: The core challenge is predicting which users will respond to ads and promotions given very little history for new campaigns. The method works because training a single model on all objectives (streams, clicks, follows) forces the model to learn shared patterns across diverse user behaviors and contexts. When the model learns what makes content appealing generally, it can apply that understanding to new advertising goals even without examples of those specific goals. The shared knowledge of user preferences and content characteristics serves as a bridge: instead of starting from scratch for a new campaign, the model transfers what it learned about persuasion and engagement from thousands of existing interactions. This reduces the cost-per-stream because the model can immediately make reasonable decisions for cold-start users rather than wasting impressions on random exploration.
976: Dynamical networks are systems where the structure itself changes based on activity—edges form or fade, weights shift—making them inherently uncertain. Quantifying uncertainty means establishing bounds on how wrong predictions could be given incomplete information about the network's current state and parameters. The guarantee comes from rigorous probability accounting: if you measure the range of plausible network structures and their dynamics, you can compute which predictions remain valid across all possibilities and which break under some but not others. This matters because networks are fragile—small changes in topology can flip a system from stable synchronization to cascading failure—so knowing the range of outcomes prevents false confidence. For epidemiology or power grids, this framework transforms vague worry into actionable risk: you know how much room for surprise exists and can design safeguards accordingly.
977: Real graphs are huge and storing them wastes memory, so the goal is creating a much smaller graph that still teaches the model the same patterns. The method works by representing many nodes as discrete codes (like hashing nodes to a codebook), then checking which nodes are structurally similar by looking at their neighborhoods. If two nodes reach the same neighbors in similar patterns, they can share the same code without breaking the model's understanding. The compact approximation captures the essential structural pathways—skipping noise—and the discrete codes make storage efficient. This works because graph patterns are hierarchical: most information flows through a small set of core structural motifs, so you can compress aggressively while preserving what the model needs to learn.
978: The attacker must inject fake nodes into a graph while fooling both the model and any defenses, which is hard because small discrete choices (add this edge or not) don't allow smooth tuning. The method sidesteps this by using reinforcement learning to treat the problem as sequential decisions rather than one-shot choices, making the discrete problem learnable. The softened numeric fingerprints smooths the discrete choices temporarily during learning, then hardens them back to valid graph changes for actual attack. This works because learning via incremental trial-and-error beats local optimization on discrete choices—the model explores many possibilities and learns what patterns of connections fool both the original model and defenses. The defense-aware policy means the learner adapts as defenses respond, rather than assuming a fixed target.
979: Knowledge bases contain patterns like 'author → paper → author' for finding collaborators, but nobody writes these patterns down explicitly. The goal is discovering which retrieval paths work best from data about what queries succeed. The approach uses a bi-level loop: one level explores which patterns might help, and another level learns how to score items using those patterns. This works because successful retrievals implicitly reveal useful patterns—if query X finds good results by following path A, that path must be relevant to understanding what query X meant. By coupling pattern discovery to retrieval success, you avoid guessing; the data itself shows you which patterns matter. This beats manual rule writing because the learned patterns adapt to what the system actually needs rather than what designers imagine.
980: Graph-based recommendation learns from user-item interactions, but random augmentation (adding fake edges or removing real ones) disrupts this signal. The method applies diffusion to gently perturb the graph: instead of random changes, it denoises a noisy version of the graph structure, preserving the compact structure that matters while erasing incidental noise. This works because diffusion naturally separates signal from noise—the core interaction patterns are robust to small perturbations while accidental correlations fade away. For long-tail items (those with few interactions), the approach uses conditional diffusion, letting global graph structure guide the denoising so that rare items inherit the statistical strength of frequent ones. This works because rare items actually do share causal patterns with frequent items; using global signal to fill gaps leverages that hidden similarity.
981: Real recommendation systems receive images, text, creator info, and user history—many different sources—but need to produce a single unified ID representing what to recommend. The challenge is aligning these sources so a user's visual preferences align with what text says about the item. The method trains a network to learn which parts of each input correspond to the same semantic meaning across modalities. This works because the world's structure is the same whether you describe it in words or pictures; if text says 'action movie' and images show explosions, they point to the same thing. By learning to recognize that correspondence and fusing the aligned signals into one ID, the system gets a richer, more reliable ranking signal than any single view alone.
982: Fake news detectors look for specific cues in articles and comments that suggest misinformation. The attack goal is appending human-like comments that fool the detector. The method uses interpretability analysis to find which words (words or concepts) the detector weighs most heavily, then prompts a language model to generate comments using those influential words. This works because detectors rely on surface patterns, and if you use the exact language patterns the detector associates with fake news or real news, you can mislead it. The underlying principle is that detectors are only as robust as the least common feature they trust—exploit that weak point and the entire judgment flips. Pairing interpretability with generation ensures the attack is both targeted and credible rather than random noise.
983: News believability depends on subtle cues: causal language, qualifications, acknowledging counterevidence. The attack makes small, targeted edits—removing qualifiers, shifting causality, hiding caveats—that shift readers' trust in the story. This works because human judgment of credibility relies on these linguistic markers as heuristics; people subconsciously trust language that acknowledges complexity and doubt words that oversimplify. By making minimal, context-aware changes, the attack preserves the surface story so casual readers miss the manipulation, while the edits systematically weaken the linguistic signals of careful reporting. This exploits the gap between what a headline literally says and the tone of authority it conveys.
984: Code generation requires multiple skills in sequence: understanding the problem, choosing an algorithm, describing the solution, then writing code. Current benchmarks only measure the final result, missing where reasoning breaks. The approach breaks evaluation into phases and measures each separately. This works because skills are interdependent—a weak choice of algorithm dooms the code even if syntax is perfect, and weak problem understanding ruins algorithm selection at the root. By measuring each phase independently, you see where models actually fail, not just whether the final output runs. This reveals that progress in one phase directly enables progress in the next, showing that the path to improvement is building the earlier skills first.
985: When judging whether an article is relevant multiple times, starting guess judgments unconsciously bias later ones—you expect consistency even when items genuinely differ. Psychological research shows certain personality traits reduce this bias. The method simulates these personality profiles in the language model through prompting. This works because personality profiles encode stable reasoning patterns: someone high in openness considers diverse perspectives and is less rigid in applying first impressions; someone low in neuroticism stays calm and doesn't spiral into anxiety-driven confirmation bias. By instilling these reasoning patterns through the prompt, the model carries them through the judgment sequence, naturally reducing the pressure to match earlier answers.
986: Auditing YouTube's recommendations requires mimicking real users at scale while staying reproducible, but real users are chaotic. The framework uses language models to simulate coherent user personas with consistent interests and behaviors. This works because coherent personas reveal systematic patterns in how algorithms personalize: instead of each user being random noise, you see how the algorithm responds to consistent signals. Personas are reproducible—run them again and get the same context—while still being realistic enough to trigger genuine algorithmic behavior. Decoupling contexts from personas means you can isolate what matters: is the algorithm reacting to stated preferences, viewing history, or both? This design turns a black-box system into an auditable one.
987: Portfolio optimization is constrained by the user's comfort with risk: someone might accept a volatile strategy if it offers higher returns, or might refuse it. The goal is generating diverse portfolios that respect the user's risk appetite. Traditional approaches either optimize for one solution (rigid) or forecast time series, then optimize (complex and misaligned). The method treats the portfolio itself as something to sample from a distribution, not as a point to find. This works because diffusion naturally generates diverse samples while respecting constraints: during denoising, you specify the risk level as a conditioning signal that guides the denoising toward portfolios matching that risk. This is simpler than forecasting futures because you directly learn the distribution of good portfolios from data rather than trying to predict what markets will do.
988: Attacking a recommender system means injecting fake users that shift recommendations. Existing attacks use simple heuristics or brute-force exploration. The method uses language models to behave like realistic users, generating ratings and reviews that feel authentic. This works because recommender systems learn from behavioral signals: if a fake user rates and reviews items coherently, the system treats it as real signal rather than obvious manipulation. Language models trained on human review patterns can generate text that mimics authentic voice and reasoning, bypassing the casual scrutiny that catches obviously fake content. By combining strategic fake-user profiles with realistic behavior generation, the attack becomes stealthier while having more impact than methods that either oversimplify or require insider knowledge.
989: Language models can rank items and explain why, but their explanations often miss the real reasons they rank something high—the reasoning sounds plausible but disconnected from what the model actually learned about user preferences.
