This benchmark's value lies in isolating integration failure from retrieval failure, exposing that language model web search still requires fundamental improvements in reading comprehension, not just tool availability. The cost-accuracy trade-off is practically important for deployment in low-resource regions with metered bandwidth.
1451: Graph-Enhanced Sentence Retrieval improves abstractive summarization in low-resource languages by first extracting sentences that matter most, sidestepping generation hallucination entirely. The soundness is direct: extracted sentences are guaranteed to appear in source documents, making the summary faithful by construction. The method scales to low-resource languages through a mixture-of-experts design: instead of one large model, multiple small experts collaborate, each specializing in linguistic phenomena common to certain language families. Adding graph structure modeling discourse relationships lets the model score sentences not just by content but by how they connect to surrounding sentences, improving extraction coherence. With only 3.2M parameters, training completes on a single GPU and fits available budgets. This approach trades elegant end-to-end generation for faithful, compute-efficient extraction, a pragmatic compromise when truthfulness and resources matter more than stylistic polish.
1452: This study trains a text classifier to distinguish AI language systems-generated answers from human-written answers on agricultural questions in Swahili. The method works because language models generate text with consistent statistical properties: longer sequences, lower word-diversity patterns, and measurable similarity to their training data all appear reliably in generated text. A logistic regression classifier learns these patterns and achieves 0.98 accuracy, proving the patterns are strong and learnable. The 0.98 accuracy signals that generated answers exhibit fingerprints of their origin. This detectability matters for IR system evaluation: when answers come from language models, knowing which ones are generated versus human-expert answers lets evaluators adjust their trust and audit output quality. In low-resource agricultural settings where misinformation spreads rapidly and farmer welfare depends on answer reliability, detectability becomes a diagnostic tool for assurance.
1453: Tulun combines machine translation with language model post-editing, guided by user-maintained translation memories and domain glossaries, to improve technical translation for low-resource languages like Tetun and Bislama. The system works because translation memory and glossaries anchor terminology: if a specialized term appears in translation memory with its starting guess correct translation, fetching and using that example in the language model prompt improves consistency and accuracy. Domain granularity matters because medical terminology differs radically from general discourse; broad categories miss this specificity. The 16-22 ChrF++ point improvement comes from in-context learning: the language model corrects and contextualizes machine-translation output when shown relevant domain examples. Transparency to end-users is crucial because it lets them understand why choices were made and refine glossaries, creating a human-in-the-loop cycle. This retrieval-augmented approach succeeds where traditional machine translation alone fails on technical domains.
1454: Morphology-Aware Retrieval for Shona addresses a fundamental linguistic challenge: Shona is a morphologically complex language where words combine stems with prefixes and suffixes that carry grammatical information. Standard English-tuned retrieval methods treat these words as atomic units and fail to recognize that two Shona sentences with different surface words may express the same meaning through morphological variation. Retrieval requires matching semantically equivalent forms, so a method must decompose words into meaningful parts or learn their relationships from training data. A large-scale benchmark dataset lets researchers train and test methods specifically on Shona morphology, measuring whether morphology-aware approaches outperform generic dense retrieval. This benchmark removes the perception that Shona is too small or obscure to work on and creates the objective yardstick needed to build inclusive tools. Equitable digital access depends on having language-specific methods where linguistic structure demands them.
1455: The core problem is ranking educational documents by relevance when the school itself must host retrieval without internet. The underlying principle is that a ranking method works only if it considers what matters in the specific context—here, both the content match to a query and alignment with the actual curriculum taught. This principle applies because teachers and learners use the system within a defined educational scope; a document relevant to physics but outside their grade level wastes limited storage and time. By explicitly modeling both textual similarity and curriculum position, the system ensures results match not just queries but real teaching goals, solving the fundamental constraint: offline systems cannot learn from click logs or A/B tests, so ranking must rest on domain structure from the start.
1456: The task is identifying which laws apply to a specific case—a discrete matching problem. The core insight is that the citation structure of cases is evidence of relevance: if many past cases cited a statute, that statute likely matters for similar future cases. This principle works because legal relevance is partly determined by historical consensus, not just text similarity. By first retrieving candidate statutes via text matching and then reranking them using the graph structure of citations, the system leverages two complementary signals: documents that mention similar words are probably in the ballpark, but documents linked through the citation network are closer to the true answer. This two-stage design solves the scarcity problem: with limited training data, combining surface similarity with structural relationships gives more trustworthy predictions than either alone.
1457: The goal is enabling retrieval in extremely low-resource languages where no digital resources yet exist. The foundational principle is that cross-lingual retrieval becomes possible when you have parallel text and speech data—equivalent sentences in two languages teach the system which concepts map across language boundaries. This principle applies because information need and expression differ from language to language, yet the underlying concepts and facts should align; a sentence about weather in Hehe should retrieve the same weather information when searched in Kiswahili. By collecting parallel corpora and speech, the project creates the minimal infrastructure on which any retrieval system can build: without these paired examples, no automated method can bridge the gap. This directly solves the access problem: speakers of small languages gain pathways to existing digital knowledge by routing through more-resourced languages as intermediaries.
1458: The core measurement is where users look when searching, and how their focus shifts when they see AI-generated answers alongside traditional links. The principle underlying eye tracking is that focus reveals cognitive effort and preference: where people look signals what they trust or find relevant, and how long they look signals processing difficulty. This principle applies because the human visual system is reflexive—people look at things they process, often before they consciously decide. By comparing where eyes go for conventional search results versus AI summaries, the study reveals whether users treat the two sources equally or show systematic bias, without relying on self-reported preferences which are often unreliable. This solves a design question: interface builders need empirical evidence of how people actually behave, not assumptions, to build search tools that adapt to the presence of AI.
1459: Scientific fact-checking requires finding evidence that either confirms or refutes a specific claim. The core principle is that evidence for verification and evidence for general relevance are not the same thing: a paper might mention the same topic but contradict the claim or be irrelevant to judging it. This principle applies because verification is a contrastive task—the retriever must find papers that could possibly weigh in on the claim, whether supporting or opposing, not merely papers topically similar. Standard ranking systems treat all relevant papers equally, but for fact-checking, a paper that takes an opposite stance is as useful as one that agrees, and both matter more than a tangentially related paper. By designing retrieval specifically for the verification task, rather than generic similarity, the system ensures downstream models receive the right evidence to reason about claim truth, solving the core bottleneck: poor evidence makes verification impossible no matter how good the verification model is.
1460: Proactive search anticipates what the user wants to ask next, rather than waiting for an explicit query. The principle is that conversation has structure: users gradually narrow or pivot their goals through dialogue, and those moves follow patterns. This principle applies because information seeking is a sequential process—each question typically depends on answers to previous ones, so the user's current position and recent queries reveal likely next moves. By inferring implicit intent from the pattern of past exchanges, a proactive system can surface relevant suggestions before the user knows to ask, reducing the burden of formulating every new query from scratch. This solves a real effort problem: in complex searches spanning many turns, users often get stuck not knowing what to ask next; offering anticipatory suggestions shortens the path to answers.
1461: Conversational retrieval tries to adapt results to each user's background and needs, but deciding when adaptation helps is itself a hard problem. The core principle is that personalisation is not uniformly beneficial: sometimes a query should be answered the same way for everyone, while other times user history dramatically changes the right answer. This principle applies because different query types have different personalisation requirements; a factual question like 'What is photosynthesis?' needs the same answer for all users, but 'What job opportunities exist for me?' depends entirely on starting guess context. By training a classifier to predict when personalisation helps for each query, and then routing through specialized agents for personalised or generic retrieval accordingly, the system avoids wasting computation and avoids diluting results with irrelevant personalization. This solves the efficiency and accuracy trade-off: systems can be both personalized and precise by adapting the degree of personalization to what each query actually requires.
1462: When an AI language systems answers a question, users need to trust that the answer is grounded in real evidence and faithful to sources cited. The core principle is that generation without verification is unreliable: AI language systems can produce plausible-sounding but false information, and they sometimes cite sources that do not actually support what they claim. This principle applies because language models are trained to predict next words based on statistical patterns, not to verify truth; they have no built-in mechanism to check whether their own outputs match reality. By requiring the system to explicitly retrieve evidence before generating an answer, check that retrieved evidence actually supports each claim, and surface uncertainty when evidence is sparse or conflicting, the system builds verification into the pipeline. This solves the decision-making problem: technical and scientific decision-makers need confidence that answers are truthful, not just confident-sounding, and explicit evidence checking is the only way to provide that.
1463: When users search in systems that blend traditional keyword search with AI chat, their strategy depends on their background knowledge and cognitive level. The principle is that deeper cognitive processing requires different information access; someone learning a topic for the first time needs different support than an expert refining understanding. This principle applies because knowledge levels affect both what users know to search for and how they interpret results: novices ask broad exploratory questions and struggle to evaluate sources, while experts ask targeted questions and can quickly judge relevance. Eye-tracking reveals these differences in focus and interaction speed. By measuring cognitive development alongside search behavior, the research shows which interface designs serve which learners, solving an educational challenge: adaptive systems can adjust between modes—guiding novices with structured exploration, letting experts quickly narrow results—based on demonstrated knowledge.
1464: Generative retrieval systems encode knowledge in model parameters, but real-world document collections grow and change constantly. The core principle is that when new information arrives, a model trained on old information must be updated without forgetting everything it already learned. This principle applies because retraining from scratch is prohibitively expensive and loses adjust knowledge, while ignoring new information makes the system stale. By applying continual learning techniques—methods that integrate new training examples while preserving performance on old knowledge—the system stays current without repeated expensive retraining. The same principle extends to temporal queries where facts have timestamps, and multimodal data where images and text evolve together. This solves the deployment problem: real retrieval systems cannot afford to rebuild monthly; they need efficient mechanisms to incorporate new documents and facts on an ongoing basis.
1465: Federated recommendation trains on user data that never leaves individual devices, but this creates extreme fragmentation: each user sees only their own history, so systems cannot directly observe which users have similar tastes. The core principle is that similar users' update patterns should influence each other more strongly than dissimilar users' patterns. This principle applies because collaborative recommendation relies on identifying users with aligned preferences, and in federated settings with only local data, the model updates themselves encode preference structure: users with similar update directions have similar tastes. By weighting aggregation based on similarity between update lists of numbers—rather than treating all users equally—the system reconstructs collaborative signals from the fragments. This solves the collaboration problem: federated systems can still learn from many users without centralizing data by recognizing that similar behavior patterns, even when observed locally and partially, reveal similar preferences.
1466: When documents contain both text and images—like research papers with figures, financial reports with tables, or medical scans with notes—the question is how to break them into retrievable pieces. The core principle is that retrieval granularity determines what can be found: if you split documents into sentences, you miss insights that require seeing a figure together with its caption. If you split by document, you can miss that Figure 3 answers the query but Figure 5 does not. This principle applies because questions about multimodal content often ask about specific elements and their relationships, not whole documents; a query might ask 'What does the graph show?' or 'Which table contains growth rates?'. By moving beyond document-level or passage-level chunking to reasoning about how to group text, images, and tables into semantically coherent units, the system makes fine-grained retrieval possible. This solves the evidence design problem: multimodal question answering fails when evidence chunks ignore the role of images and tables; chunking by informational meaning rather than document structure ensures each retrieved piece actually answers the query.
1467: Search engines now embed AI language systems to improve results, but AI language systems are expensive and sensitive to input quality and shifts in query distribution. The core principle is that components optimized for one use case—human searchers—often fail when the users change—AI agents querying systematically. This principle applies because human and AI search differ fundamentally: humans type occasional queries with typos and reformulation, while AI language systems-agents generate many queries rapidly and systematically as part of reasoning loops. Caching, spelling correction, and query understanding models all assume human query patterns; applying them to AI traffic wastes compute and can degrade results. By measuring how AI language systems actually use search—their query volume, reformulation patterns, sensitivity to noise—infrastructure designers can optimize pipeline components for dual traffic. This solves the scalability problem: as AI language systems become search users, systems that ignore this dual role will waste compute and resources; explicitly modeling both human and AI search enables more efficient infrastructure.
1468: In online discussions mixing human and AI participants, people adjust their judgments to match what others think—a tendency called conformity. The core principle is that social conformity emerges from comparison: individuals look to others' views as evidence and adjust toward the majority. This principle applies because groups create implicit pressure; when most people accept an idea, questioning it feels risky, and when AI agents align with human consensus, they appear more trustworthy. The presence and positioning of AI agents in the group alters conformity dynamics: people may conform more to a majority that includes AI, or differently if the AI disagrees with the human majority. By studying how conformity operates in mixed groups, the research reveals whether AI participation changes how trustworthy information judgments become, solving a critical concern: as AI-generated content permeates discussions, understanding whether AI presence increases or decreases collective judgment quality helps predict real-world information consequences.
1469: Weak supervision aggregates many noisy signals—like citation patterns or keyword matches—to label documents without expensive manual review. The core principle is that signals are more reliable when they come from similar contexts: a heuristic predicting relevance might work well for papers by the same author but fail for papers in a different subfield. This principle applies because citation topology reveals context: papers nearby in the citation network are likely similar in topic and standards, so a relevance heuristic developed from one cluster's citations is more trustworthy within that cluster than globally. By learning how each heuristic's reliability varies with document position in the citation network—rather than assuming uniform reliability—the system makes better use of noisy signals. This solves the scarcity problem: large-scale relevance judgments are expensive to collect, but by recognizing that different heuristics work in different contexts, systems can extract more reliable training signal from the same amount of noise.
1470: Climate change evidence synthesis requires finding relevant scientific papers across disconnected databases and domains, then combining findings into a coherent picture. The core task is matching complex information needs to scattered sources while detecting when retrieval fails silently. The mathematical principle at work is that structured provenance tracking—recording not just what documents say but where claims came from, who verified them, and what gaps remain—creates verifiable chains of reasoning that human experts can audit. This works because disagreements about evidence quality, geographic applicability, and methodological soundness cannot be resolved by statistical similarity alone; they require explicit documentation that humans can inspect. By building unified pipelines that integrate geographic data, time-series measurements, and bibliographic sources with this provenance layer, systems can transparently show where human judgment must override automated ranking, addressing the real problem that climate policy decisions demand justification visible to skeptics.
1471: Personalized search systems rank items based on user history and preferences, but small choices in how items flow through the ranking pipeline can reinforce biases or create feedback loops where popular items grow more prominent regardless of individual user needs. The soundness principle is that bias-aware ranking must measure fairness along multiple features—representation of groups, disparities in exposure, and whether minorities are systematically ranked lower—and these metrics can be optimized simultaneously only if fairness is built into the loss function that the system learns from. This principle holds because feedback loops operate through the data used for training: if past ranking choices biased toward majority groups, the model learns those patterns and amplifies them forward. By measuring unfairness directly in the ranking process, not as a post-hoc audit, systems can detect and counteract this spiral before recommendations harden into disparate outcomes. This addresses the real need: as users increasingly depend on personalized systems for access to information, those systems must not inadvertently exclude entire groups from opportunities.
1472: Real-world questions often require retrieving multiple pieces of information and combining them under logical constraints—such as finding experiments satisfying specific conditions or verifying claims against contradictory evidence. Traditional retrieval ranks by semantic similarity alone, but this cannot enforce logical soundness. The core principle is that reasoning requires explicit representation of logical structure and the inference rules that make conclusions follow necessarily from premises. This principle applies to information retrieval because real evidence does not exist in isolation: an answer is sound only if it respects the constraints of the question and synthesizes evidence coherently. Diverse approaches—from neuro-symbolic systems that interleave learning and logic, to probabilistic frameworks that track uncertainty in inference, to energy-based models that score whole reasoning chains—all embody this same insight: information systems must move beyond matching patterns to verifying that conclusions genuinely follow from retrieved premises. This soundness is essential for high-stakes domains where users must justify their decisions to others or detect when the system has made an unjustified leap.
1473: Personalized systems must adapt responses to individual contexts, goals, and histories, but this adaptation requires retrieving relevant background information and then generating responses that reflect personal circumstances. The core challenge is that generic models produce generic outputs; personalization requires conditioning the entire pipeline—retrieval, ranking, and generation—on user-specific signals. The mathematical principle underlying this is that when you decompose personalization across stages of a pipeline, each stage can be optimized independently for personalization objectives while remaining modular; this works because the output of each stage (ranked documents, generated text) becomes input to the next, allowing personalized signals to propagate forward. This principle holds as long as personalization signals are aligned across stages: if retrieval personalizes one way and generation personalizes differently, the outputs will conflict. By explicitly designing agent-based systems that plan personalized actions and adapt execution in response to user feedback, the system can recover from misalignment and learn user intent online. This addresses the practical need: deployed systems must handle users with vastly different preferences and contexts, and must adapt as those preferences evolve.
1474: Evaluating search and recommendation systems using simulated users avoids the cost of recruiting humans, but the risk is that a simulator may make choices inconsistent with its declared profile or may harbor biases against certain demographic groups. The core computational task is predicting what choice a user would make given their profile, task context, and the system's output. The soundness principle is that if you decompose the simulator into auditable, interpretable components—a persona with explicit attributes, task-level contracts that specify expected behavior, execution traces that record why each choice was made, and verification checks that confirm choices match the persona—then you can detect inconsistencies and biases by inspecting this trail. This principle works because simulated choices are functions of these components; if you can see the components and the choices they produced, you can reverse-engineer whether the simulator behaves as intended. By adding a refinement loop that updates personas and contracts based on detected inconsistencies, the framework becomes verifiable rather than opaque. This matters because biased simulators can systematically disadvantage minority groups in evaluation, leading to deployed systems that seem to perform well but actually discriminate.
1475: The field of information retrieval has fragmented into many specialized methods—lexical search, neural ranking, question answering—making it difficult for researchers to experiment with combining them. The core problem is that methods use different interfaces and data formats, creating friction when building pipelines. The insight underlying PyTerrier is that if you provide a unified abstraction layer with common operations—search, rerank, filter, combine—then researchers can mix methods without reimplementation. This principle works because information retrieval tasks are compositional: you retrieve documents, then rerank them, then extract answers, and each step takes the previous step's output as input. By standardizing this composition interface, the library lets researchers rapidly explore combinations and measure the effect of each component. This addresses the practical bottleneck: progress in IR depends on comparing methods and building on starting guess work, but friction from different implementations means researchers repeat effort and focus narrowly on single methods rather than end-to-end evaluation.
1476: Information continuously changes, and the relevance of a document depends not just on whether it contains relevant content but on when that content became true and whether it remains true today. The core problem is ranking and reasoning about information whose validity shifts over time. The mathematical principle is that temporal information extraction and retrieval require explicit normalization of time expressions into a shared timeline, allowing systems to compare when events occurred and whether they overlap with the user's question. This principle applies because temporal reasoning relies on precise comparison: without normalization, the system cannot detect that two documents refer to the same event at different times or determine causality across events. By treating time as a first-class features in extraction, retrieval, and generation, systems can enforce temporal consistency—answering not just what is true but what was true when and whether it still holds. This is essential for reasoning systems because incorrect temporal assumptions lead to contradictions: a system might retrieve conflicting information without realizing the statements refer to different time periods.
1477: Recommender systems must combine relevance, user preferences, and multi-step reasoning to suggest actions such as purchasing items or making reservations. The core challenge is coordinating multiple agents, each handling specialized subtasks—understanding user intent, searching inventory, comparing options, executing transactions—while keeping decisions aligned with user goals. The principle enabling this is that if agents can call tools, observe results, and iteratively refine their plans, they can solve multi-step problems that no single agent could solve in one pass. This works because real decisions require gathering information sequentially: an agent first learns the user's budget and preferences, then searches for items, then compares options, adapting its plan as it learns what is available. By explicitly orchestrating this multi-agent process, the system can surface intermediate steps to the user and incorporate feedback that corrects course. This addresses deployment challenges: industrial systems must handle diverse user goals and unusual requests, and must do so transparently so users understand and can override the system's reasoning.
1478: Language models generate generic responses because they lack user-specific information; personalization requires encoding individual preferences, memories, and contexts into the model's decision process. The core problem is that preferences are individual—no universal ranking of options is correct for all users—so the model must somehow condition its output on personal data. The principle enabling this is that personalization can be applied at multiple points in the model's lifecycle: during training through curating or reweighting examples toward individual preferences, during inference through conditioning on retrieved personal context or user history, and through memory systems that track evolving preferences over time. This principle works because each layer of personalization amplifies the signal from the previous layer: a model adjust on one user's preferences learns that user's values, and then at inference time conditioning on that user's recent interactions further narrows the output. By combining these layers—memory, architecture, training objectives, inference adaptation—systems can align model behavior with individual goals while remaining practical to deploy at scale. This matters because generic systems cannot serve diverse users well; personalization is necessary for systems to respect individual autonomy and provide value tailored to context.
1479: E-commerce platforms must retrieve and rank products to maximize both relevance to user queries and business objectives such as inventory turnover and sponsored placement. Unlike web search where relevance is primarily topical, e-commerce relevance depends on product attributes, user purchase history, price, and availability, creating a distinct ranking problem. The core challenge is measuring success—traditional IR metrics like click-through rate may not reflect user satisfaction or business health—and deciding how to balance organic results against sponsored recommendations. The principle at work is that e-commerce ranking functions must optimize multiple objectives simultaneously: relevance, diversity to prevent redundant recommendations, and fairness to avoid favoring sellers who pay for placement. This principle applies because users need diverse options to choose from, and trust erodes if rankings appear manipulated; simultaneously, platforms must generate revenue and sellers must have opportunities to reach customers. By explicitly measuring interaction patterns like cart additions and purchases rather than clicks alone, and by designing ranking functions that trade off these objectives transparently, platforms can optimize for both user and business value. This addresses the applied problem: real platforms operate in mixed incentive environments where naive optimization of a single metric leads to poor user experiences or unsustainable business models.
1480: As ranking and recommendation systems become more complex and consequential, users deserve to understand how systems made their decisions. Explainability requires systems to expose their reasoning in human-interpretable form, creating accountability. The core problem is that modern systems use many distributed signals—learned representations, statistical patterns, multiple ranking stages—making it hard to point to a single reason for an outcome. The principle enabling explainability is that if you decompose the system into interpretable stages and measure the contribution of each stage to the final ranking, you can construct explanations that show which factors mattered most. This principle works because ranking is compositional: documents pass through multiple filters and scoring stages, and by measuring the impact of each stage you can trace how a high-ranked item rose in the ranking. By building transparency and explainability into system design rather than bolting it on afterward, systems become auditable: users can detect whether rankings reflect their interests or the system's biases, and designers can identify and fix failure modes before deployment. This addresses the societal need: as systems make decisions affecting access to opportunities, users and regulators must be able to verify those decisions are sound.
1481: Conversational systems must maintain context across multiple turns—understanding what the user has already asked, what they learned, and how their information need is evolving—while retrieving relevant information to answer follow-up questions. The core challenge is that context grows over time, so the system must decide what information remains relevant and how to efficiently rank documents given the full conversation history. The principle enabling this is that if systems maintain an explicit conversation state representing what the user has learned and what they still seek, they can use that state to personalize retrieval and ranking for each new query. This principle applies because follow-up questions are abbreviated: users assume the system remembers context, so a question like What about in that region requires the system to recall previous discussion to understand what region means. By explicitly tracking conversation state and using it to modify retrieval and ranking, systems can handle these abbreviated questions and adapt their explanations to the user's knowledge level. This addresses practical needs: users prefer concise follow-up questions, and systems must parse abbreviations correctly; additionally, users appreciate personalized explanations that build on what they already know rather than starting from scratch.
1482: Neural retrieval models improve ranking quality but consume substantial memory and computation, making them expensive to run as first-stage retrievers at scale. The core problem is that efficiency and effectiveness are often in tension: more complex models achieve higher ranking quality but cost more to run. The principle enabling efficient retrieval is that many tasks do not require maximum effectiveness—a small reduction in ranking quality for a large reduction in cost may be acceptable—so the question becomes how to measure this efficiency-effectiveness tradeoff systematically. This principle works because efficiency gains come from multiple sources: simpler models, faster inference hardware, reduced model size through compression, or approximate retrieval that skips some candidates. By establishing shared benchmarks and evaluation protocols where efficiency and effectiveness are measured alongside each other, the community can compare tradeoffs fairly and incentivize the development of practical methods. This addresses a deployment bottleneck: IR methods are not adopted at scale unless they work within operational budgets, so advancing efficiency is as important as advancing effectiveness; yet the community has lacked common measurement standards that make this tradeoff visible and comparable.
1483: Information ecosystems now contain both human-authored and AI-generated content, but retrieval systems were designed assuming corpora contain only human text. The core problem is that AI-generated content may contain hallucinations or be weakly grounded, yet ranking systems cannot easily distinguish it from human content, potentially ranking false or misleading information high. The principle at work is that evaluation metrics designed for human corpora measure different properties than those designed for synthetic content: metrics like relevance to a query work for both, but metrics like factual accuracy or credibility require measuring whether claims are grounded in external evidence. This principle applies because synthetic content poses new risks: a hallucinated but plausible-sounding answer might rank high because it is fluent and mentions relevant terms, even if false. By explicitly studying the properties of AI-generated content and redesigning evaluation to measure both quality and provenance, systems can more fairly rank mixed content and alert users to reliability concerns. This addresses emerging challenges: as synthetic content proliferates, systems that ignore its distinctive properties will inadvertently promote misinformation; evaluation frameworks must evolve to handle mixed corpora where human judgment about credibility is essential.
1484: Information retrieval systems embody choices about whose information is made visible, whose voice is amplified, and how access is mediated, making them political tools. The core problem is that IR researchers have typically treated their systems as neutral technical artifacts, ignoring how design choices affect power and access. The principle at work is that systems designed without explicit focus to social justice and democratic values will tend to reinforce existing inequalities: algorithms amplify trends in training data, platforms favor content that attracts engagement over truth, and corporate control of search platforms concentrates power over information access. This principle applies because information is fundamental to participation and freedom: communities without access to information cannot advocate for themselves, and communities whose perspectives are systematically downranked have less influence over shared decisions. By explicitly centering questions of emancipation and democratic values in system design, researchers can ask whether their choices serve oppressive or liberatory aims and redesign toward more equitable alternatives. This addresses fundamental needs: societies depend on accessible, trustworthy information systems for democracy to function, so IR research that ignores justice concerns is complicit in systems of oppression.
1485: The core task is identifying and cataloging failure modes in systems that generate text for search. The soundness rests on this principle: when many independent researchers study the same systems from different angles—adversarial, behavioral, fairness—they uncover different slices of real harm that no single perspective catches. This works because generative systems fail in surprising, non-obvious ways that only become visible when you combine attack intuition, empirical testing, and domain knowledge from security and social science. By synthesizing these views, the community builds a shared map of what can go wrong, which is essential for preventing deployment disasters where an untested vulnerability leads to user harm at scale.
1486: The core problem is matching executable agents to user needs in a world where agents can fail, behave unpredictably, or have hidden constraints. The key insight is that traditional ranking methods—which score documents by relevance—fail here because agents are dynamic: their usefulness depends on what the user actually wants them to do, what they're capable of, and whether they'll complete the task correctly. By building systems that index agents by their stated capabilities and observed behaviors, then re-score them according to multi-dimensional criteria (accuracy, speed, cost, safety), retrieval becomes possible. This works because it shifts focus from treating agents as passive information to treating them as systems with measurable, comparable properties that can be checked before deployment.
1487: The core task is learning what a user wants from their interactions and language, then using that learned profile to improve future recommendations. This is powerful because AI language systems can summarize and reason about user history in natural language—they extract patterns humans can understand (this user likes papers on robotics by authors from MIT) instead of opaque numbers. The method works because language-based reasoning lets you combine explicit signals (what the user said), implicit signals (what they clicked), and external knowledge (what's currently relevant) in the same reasoning step. This soundness matters: a profile you can read and debug is far safer and more trustworthy than a black-box alternative, especially when privacy and fairness questions arise.
1488: The core task is judging whether a system successfully generated or retrieved content that matches a user's request across text, images, audio, or video. The challenge is that no single evaluation metric works: human ratings disagree, automatic metrics miss subtle failures, and the right definition of success depends on whether you're building search, recommendation, or knowledge-driven tasks. This workshop's approach works because it brings together specialists in language, vision, and evaluation who each understand where their single discipline's metrics break down. By pooling these views and running shared benchmarks, the community can move toward evaluation standards that actually predict whether a multimodal system will satisfy real users, rather than optimizing for a metric that looks good on paper.
